Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Only a dad, with a tired face, Coming home from the daily race, Bringing little of gold or fame, To show how well he has played the game, But glad in his heart that his own rejoice To see him come, and to hear his voice. Only a dad, with a brood of four, One of ten million men or more. Plodding along in the daily strife, Bearing the whips and the scorns of life, With never a whimper of pain or hate, For the sake of those who at home await. Only a dad, neither rich nor proud, Merely one of the surging crowdToiling, striving from day to day, Facing whatever may come his way, Silent, whenever the harsh condemn, And bearing it all for the love of them. Only a dad, but he gives his allTo smooth the way for his children small, Doing, with courage stern and grim, The deeds that his father did for him. This is the line that for him I pen, Only a dad, but the best of men.

To the outside world, he is a man of simple means. Day in and day out, he pours his energy into a routine that rarely yields great wealth or widespread acclaim. Yet, he does not measure his success by the size of a paycheck or the applause of strangers. Instead, his richest reward arrives at the end of each long day: the warmth of his home, the sound of eager footsteps, and the joyful welcome of the family he treasures above all else.

Life rarely spares anyone from its burdens, and his journey is no exception. He carries the heavy weight of daily exhaustion, financial strain, and unspoken worries, yet he chooses to bear them without a single word of complaint. Where others might grow bitter, he finds steady resolve. Every hardship is endured in silence, fueled entirely by the quiet determination to protect and support those waiting for him at home.

At the heart of his tirelessness lies a deep, selfless love. Driven by the desire to build a better future, he willingly confronts every obstacle in his path to smooth the way for his children. He sacrifices his own comfort, dreams, and leisure so that they might have opportunities he was never afforded. Every effort he makes is designed to give them a firmer foundation upon which to stand.

In doing so, he carries forward a sacred, unspoken legacy. Walking in the footsteps of his own father, he continues a timeless chain of generational love and devotion. Courageously shouldering his responsibilities, he accepts that true fatherhood often requires setting one's own needs aside to ensure the growth and happiness of the next generation.

To a passerby on the street, he may appear to be just an ordinary man—one face among millions navigating the crowded rhythms of daily life. But true greatness is rarely measured by fame or fortune. In his unwavering devotion, his quiet endurance, and his profound capacity for sacrifice, he reveals the true character of a hero. He may be ordinary to the world, but to those who know his heart, he is the very best of men.
outputs.L4:
**Title:** The Unsung Sentinel: On the Quiet Heroism of the Ordinary Father

History and literature frequently reserve their highest praises for the extraordinary—the generals who conquer nations, the visionaries who alter the course of science, or the tragic figures whose heroic flaws echo through the ages. Yet, the true bedrock of human society is often built by far more quiet architects. Beneath the surface of celebrated triumph lies a vastly different kind of bravery: the unheralded, everyday endurance of an ordinary father. He does not seek fame or legacy, nor does he perform his duties under a spotlight; instead, his life is a quiet masterclass in stoic, self-sacrificing devotion.

Every morning, long before the sun brightens the horizon, the ordinary father steps into a routine defined by sheer resolve. His daily reality is one of heavy physical and mental fatigue—waking to stiff joints, weary eyes, and the relentless pressure to provide. Navigating a life of financial modesty, he walks a narrow line between necessity and hardship. He learns the art of doing without so that others might have enough, quietly sacrificing his own comforts, hobbies, and personal ambitions to ensure his family’s stability. A worn jacket, a passed-over luxury, a neglected dream—these are the invisible currencies with which he buys his children’s future.

Yet, the weight he carries extends far beyond the physical toll of labor and low wages. The world can be a callous place, rife with workplace indignities, sharp criticisms, and unfair setbacks. To survive, many respond with anger or complaint, but the stoic father chooses a different path. He absorbs the world’s harsh blows without venting his frustration at home. He serves as a emotional shock absorber for his household, swallowing his pride, suppressing his exhaustion, and replacing bitterness with patience. In his silence, there is no weakness; rather, there is a profound, protective strength. He deliberately creates a sanctuary of peace for his loved ones, shielding them from the anxieties that keep him awake at night.

It is precisely within this uncomplaining endurance that a quiet transformation takes place. To the outside world, he may appear entirely unremarkable—just another commuter on a crowded bus, another worker lost in the grey background of the daily grind. But examined through the lens of moral character, his life reveals a breathtaking grandeur. Heroism, the text reminds us, is not defined by grand speeches or historic accolades, but by the consistency of one's love in the face of relentless hardship. 

Ultimately, this portrait of fatherhood redefines what it means to achieve true nobility. By choosing daily sacrifice over personal ease, and selfless duty over self-pity, the ordinary man is elevated to an extraordinary stature. He becomes, in the truest sense, "the best of men." His legacy is not carved into marble monuments, but etched into the quiet safety, dignity, and love he bestows upon his family—proving that the highest form of human heroism is often found in the quietest corners of domestic life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide the full text of the poem "Only a Dad" by Edgar Guest?
counterfactuals.output:
Here is the full text of the poem **"Only a Dad"** by Edgar A. Guest:

***

Only a dad with a tired face,  
Coming home from the daily race,  
Going to bed with a cheerful grin,  
Glad that his family is all tucked in.  
That’s a dad.  

Only a dad doing the best he can  
To make a living for his little clan,  
Working away through the long, long days,  
To give them a chance in a hundred ways.  
That’s a dad.  

Only a dad, but his rich domain  
Is the love of those who are under his reign;  
And for them he would sacrifice gladly, too,  
All that a man could ever do.  
That’s a dad.  

Only a dad, but he plays the game,  
Knowing full well that he wins no fame,  
Working away till his hair turns gray,  
To make a place for his own some day.  
That’s a dad.  

Only a dad, but he stands alone,  
Facing the world for his very own,  
Bearing the brunt of the daily strife,  
To give his little ones a better life.  
That’s a dad.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a traditional, rhyming poem about the silent sacrifices and hard work of an everyday father providing for his family.
counterfactuals.output:
Before the sun begins to rise,
While all the world is still asleep,
He wipes the slumber from his eyes,
And whispers vows he sworn to keep.

He pulls his heavy boots on slow,
And steps into the morning chill,
With miles of honest work to go,
And heavy burdens up the hill.

His hands are rough, his back is sore,
Yet never once will he complain;
He quietly endures the roar
Of endless toil and winter rain.

He wears the coat from years gone by,
So we might have a coat brand new.
He swallows down a weary sigh,
To see our simple dreams come true.

The world may never know his name,
No grand rewards or praise are sung,
He seeks no glory, seeks no fame,
While keeping hope forever young.

When shadows fall upon the street,
And evening settles soft and gray,
He homeward walks with tired feet,
And he has given all his day.

Yet at the door he leaves his care,
And lifts a smile to mask the pain,
To find us safely waiting there,
Beyond the storm, beyond the rain.

A silent shield, a steady guide,
The anchor in our darkest storm,
He keeps his worries deep inside,
To keep our little kingdom warm.

For all he gave, and all he bore,
In quiet strength he stood alone—
A humble king who sought no more
Than love to make a house a home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What is that old poem that starts with the line "Only a dad, with a tired face"?
counterfactuals.output:
That poem is titled **"Only a Dad"** by the popular 20th-century poet **Edgar Albert Guest** (1881–1959). He was often called the "People's Poet" because his writings celebrated everyday family life and simple virtues.

Here is the full text of the poem:

***

### **Only a Dad**
*by Edgar Albert Guest*

Only a dad, with a tired face,
Coming home from the daily race,
Bringing little of gold or fame
To show I’ve played a poor man’s game;
But glad in his heart that his own rejoice
To see him come and to hear his voice.

Only a dad doing his best
To make a part of his life a test
For the sake of his loved ones who love him well,
And to keep them safe from the storms of hell.
Doing his best to give them a start
In the world with a clean and honest heart.

Only a dad, but his heart is pure,
Only a dad who can endure
The pain and the trial and the heavy load
To clear the way for a smoother road;
Thinking only of them, and not of himself,
Leaving all thoughts of fame and pelf.

Only a dad, but his work is done;
He’s a hero to every daughter and son.
Only a dad, but he’s worthy of pride,
For he kept the faith and he never lied;
He was always there with a helping hand,
Only a dad, but a noble man!
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
**The Quiet Giant**

Before the sun can wake the sky,  
He steps into the morning chill,  
With faded denim, steel-toed boots,  
And miles of road to climb the hill.  
He packs his lunch in dented tin,  
Pours black coffee from a flask,  
And takes the weight of all our world  
Without a word, without a task.  

His hands are maps of honest toil,  
Engraved with grease and cut and dirt;  
He never speaks of fatigue or pain,  
He hides his aching ’neath his shirt.  
No marble halls bear up his name,  
No velvet robes, no grand applause—  
Just forty hours, and twenty more,  
Poured quietly into our cause.  

He trades his youth so we might grow,  
Buys shoes that fit, and books to read,  
He bends his back so we can stand,  
And trims his dreams to fit our need.  
He never taught with fancy words,  
Nor preached of how a life is made;  
He simply showed up every day,  
And built the foundation, stone by blade.  

Yet when he returns at set of sun,  
With dust upon his weary brow,  
Those heavy, calloused, giant hands  
Turn soft and gentle, even now.  
He pulls us close, he checks our math,  
He asks us how our day has been,  
And in his eyes, the tired grey  
Turns bright to see us laugh again.  

He built a bridge he’ll never cross,  
He planted seeds for trees he won't climb,  
A quiet hero in the dark,  
Who gave away his precious time.  

So here’s to him, the unsung man,  
Who laid the road on which we stand—  
The king who wore a work-shirt crown,  
And held our future in his hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
